headline: Captree dock talk: night eels working, and the bay finally got its peanut bunker
subhead: Rough ocean pushed the bite inside this week — the inlet and the back bays are where the real work's getting done.
body_markdown:
I had a guy at the Captree fuel dock Wednesday morning ask me, half-joking, if the ocean forgot how to lay down. Fair question. We've had a lumpy Bight all week — 2.6-footers rolling in on a short six-second period, water out there pushing 79 degrees on the surface, which sounds nice until you realize that's bathwater for stripers and it's got the whole food chain either sulking deep or ducking inside where it's cooler. So that's where I sent him. That's where I've been sending everybody.

The thermal split right now is the whole story. Ocean's warm and sloppy, but Great South Bay and the inlet channels are running a few degrees under that, and any current seam that pulls cooler water past structure is going to hold fish. Fire Island Inlet on the last two hours of the outgoing has been the move — that's when the bay dumps its warmer surface water out through Democrat Point and the deeper, cooler stuff gets pulled up the channel edges. Bass are stacking there but they're not stupid about it. Daytime is basically a non-event unless you're right on that current break at first light. Real bite window is dusk into full dark, eels drifted or slow-trolled along the sod bank edges off Democrat Point and down toward the Robert Moses bridge pilings. Nothing heroic size-wise — mostly 26 to 32 inches, a few overslot fish mixed in for guys willing to sit out there past midnight — but it's a real bite if you're patient and quiet about it.

Fluke are still the most honest fish in the bay right now, and the full moon this week actually helped that fishery more than it hurt it. Bigger tidal swing means sharper current at the changes, and that's exactly when the doormats decide to feed. Best water's been the channel edges around the Robert Moses bridges, 25 to 35 feet, and the deeper cuts off Kismet and Oak Beach on the bay side. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, some guys tipping with a strip of squid for the scent trail, dragged slow right on the bottom through the last hour of the outgoing. We're seeing fish to five and six pounds mixed in with a lot of teen-and-under shorts, so it's a sort-through fishery, but the keeper ratio's been fair for August. If you're marking bait on the meter and not getting bit, move — the fluke are sitting tight to the drop, not spread across the flat.

Now here's something worth flagging — we said a couple weeks back that peanut bunker were pushing down from New England and would be in the bay inside of two weeks, and sure enough they showed up in the back creeks off Patchogue and around the Bellport flats this week. That bait push is exactly why the snapper blues and cocktail blues have gone from scattered to genuinely thick in the back bay. If you've got kids or you just want steady bend-in-the-rod action, small silver spoons or a bare hook with a sliver of bunker off any dock from Babylon to Sayville will keep you busy for an hour straight. The bigger adult blues are still tucked in tighter to the inlet and the ocean-side bars, ambushing those bunker schools on the move, so if you want a real fish on top instead of snappers, work the surf line at Democrat Point right at first light before the sun gets up and pushes everything down.

Weakfish have been a ghost story again this summer — I've heard of a couple caught incidentally on bucktails meant for fluke, nothing worth planning a trip around. Porgies are around the Fire Island reef structure and the bridge rubble in decent numbers on bloodworms and clam, but nobody's writing home about it either. Blackfish are still weeks off — don't waste bait on them yet.

One more thing worth knowing if you're a night owl: Heckscher State Park opened up Field 6 for night fishing this summer, first year ever, and it's legit — Friday, Saturday, Sunday, dusk to dawn, through Labor Day. You need a Night Sport Fishing Permit or the 4x4 permit on your dash, but if you've got it, that stretch of Great South Bay shoreline on the outgoing tide is worth a look for bass and blues working the channel edge in the dark, especially with the bay pushing that warmer water out past the marsh. It's a trial, so don't be the guy who ruins it for everybody — pack out your trash, follow the hours.

Looking ahead, the moon's coming off full and the tides will settle back to normal by the weekend, which should tighten up the bite windows again instead of spreading current out over a longer swing. If the ocean lays down even a little, I'd be watching the outer bars off Fire Island for the first sign of false albacore or bonito working bait balls — the surface temp's been sitting right in that window for a couple weeks now. Nothing confirmed yet, but that's exactly the kind of August surprise this beat throws at you when you're not looking.
